title: Full-Chain Compromise of a Regional E-Commerce Platform
summary: A self-initiated responsible disclosure engagement uncovering unauthenticated account takeover (including admin accounts), two independent SQL injection vulnerabilities, and exposure of live third-party payment and messaging credentials across two separate customer databases.

timeline.summary: Subdomain enumeration, port scan, and full authentication flow testing (login, signup, password reset) uncovered the first IDOR cluster and the account-takeover primitive.
Differential testing on an address-deletion endpoint isolated a boolean-based blind SQL injection in its pre-delete validation query.

Database name, schema, and table structure extracted via blind boolean injection; a second, UNION-based injection was independently discovered on a related endpoint, yielding direct row-level data access.
Attempts to escalate to file write, UDF-based code execution, and privilege escalation were all tested and found blocked by database-level privilege restrictions.
Cross-schema enumeration from the same injection point revealed a second, independent application database containing live third-party API credentials and a separate 1,100+ record customer base.
Findings compiled into a structured technical report and executive summary; outreach initiated across multiple public contact channels to establish a secure disclosure point of contact.

confidentiality.summary: Unauthenticated read access to full customer PII across two separate databases, plus administrator credential hashes and live third-party API secrets.

integrity.summary: Unauthenticated write access to any user's cart, address, and profile data, including the ability to alter the phone number of any account — including administrator accounts.

availability.summary: No direct denial-of-service vector confirmed; cart/address tampering could disrupt individual order fulfillment but did not threaten platform-wide availability.

privacy.summary: Full names, national ID numbers, phone numbers, physical addresses, and financial balance data exposed for well over a thousand individuals across two customer databases.

regulatory.summary: Data categories exposed fall within scope of Kenya's Data Protection Act, 2019; a real-world exploitation would very likely constitute a notifiable breach.

operational.summary: Live payment gateway and messaging provider credentials were confirmed exposed, creating a live operational risk independent of the underlying application vulnerabilities.

lessons.summary: Never change more than one variable per test window once inside a live chain — an overlapping injection attempt and a checkout test in the same session produced an anomaly that cost a full phase to (eventually) explain away.
Stop pulling rows the moment a read primitive is proven. A count query or a single representative record demonstrates impact as well as a bulk dump does, without the added exposure.

Live, currently-usable credentials (payment gateways, messaging providers) are a different risk category from static data exposure — they represent active capability, not just leaked information, and should be triaged and communicated with more urgency.
The presence of admin accounts inside the same table as ordinary users, distinguished only by a flag, meant an unrelated authorization bug automatically became an admin-account-takeover bug.

Self-initiated disclosure to an organization with no published security contact is materially slower than a defined bug bounty program — outreach had to be spread across a contact form, WhatsApp, and a social media page simultaneously just to establish a channel.

seo.description: Case study: a self-initiated responsible disclosure engagement against a regional e-commerce platform, uncovering unauthenticated account takeover, two independent SQL injection vulnerabilities, and live third-party credential exposure across two separate customer databases.
